tria-048.title: A third extinction closes the Early Triassic
tria-048.text: Life had been knocked back twice since the Permian, and now it happened a third time. A new extinction event struck at the Olenekian–Anisian boundary, ending the Early Triassic. Siberian Traps activity has been linked to it. The same volcanic source has also been tied to later crises in the Middle–Late Anisian and at the Anisian–Ladinian boundary.

tria-049.title: Pangaea starts to tear along the future Atlantic
tria-049.text:
The Atlantic Ocean began as a string of rift valleys. Shortly after the Siberian Traps eruptions ended, around 247 million years ago, the crust started pulling apart; rift sediments in the Fundy and Argana basins date to then. Extension began in the northern Central Atlantic in the Anisian and in the southern part in the Carnian. By 230 million years ago, new rift valleys had formed and filled.

From about 227 to 202 million years ago, deep half-graben basins between New Jersey and Morocco held large rift lakes, red beds and shales: the Newark Supergroup. Rifting spread to Newfoundland and Iberia, the eastern Mediterranean, and southwestern Gondwana and Patagonia, opening basins such as the Lusitanian and Cuyo. Three-armed grabens joined into the future Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Yet Pangaea had not separated. Laurasia parted from Gondwana only between 215 and 175 million years ago.

tria-045.title: Luoping fossils track the seas' revival
tria-045.text: The sea was coming back to life, and Yunnan, China, kept the evidence. The Luoping biota, about 247–245 million years old, preserves varied marine animals that record the recovery of sea life after the extinction. It is one of a series of Triassic Chinese marine biotas, alongside the older Guiyang biota.

tria-043.title: The first stony corals, tomorrow's reef builders
tria-043.text: Every Mesozoic and modern reef rests on one group of animals: the scleractinians, or stony corals. They first appeared in the late Anisian. Their big break came later, during {{ref:tria-066}}, when they diversified rapidly. That burst is linked to symbiotic dinoflagellates, called zooxanthellae, settling in their tissues as partners. Reefs built by modern-type stony corals first became relatively common in the Carnian. Even so, these corals did not become the dominant reef builders until the end of the Triassic.

tria-040.title: Archosaurs push the mammal relatives aside
tria-040.text: At first archosaurs were the underdogs, rarer than the therapsids. They began displacing them in the mid-Triassic and were the dominant land vertebrates by the Middle Triassic. From the early Triassic they took most medium to large meat-eating roles on land. Over 35 million years they came to include crocodylomorphs, pterosaurs and dinosaurs. Crocodile-line pseudosuchians dominated, from plant-eating aetosaurs to big 'rauisuchian' predators, while dinosauromorphs shared the land. Large cynodonts such as traversodontids still held some big plant-eater and predator roles.

cret-065.title: Vista Alegre crater scars Brazil's basalts
cret-065.text: An impact punched into the basalt plains of southern Brazil, near the Vargeão Dome. The Vista Alegre crater lies in those dark volcanic rocks. Geologists have only recently dated it, to about 115 million years ago, in the Early Cretaceous.
